episode_title: 720. Revolution in the Soviet Empire: Revenge of the Red Army (Part 2)

real_qa.q: What concessions did Imre Nagy offer to Hungarian revolutionaries on October 28, 1956?
real_qa.r: On October 28, Nagy offered to recognize the just demands of the people, ordered security forces to stop firing, granted amnesty to all involved in the uprising, restored old national holidays and the Hungarian flag, abolished the secret police, and ordered Soviet troops to return to their barracks with talks planned for full Red Army withdrawal from Hungarian soil.

real_qa.q: What happened at the secret police headquarters in Moson Magyarovar on October 26, 1956?
real_qa.r: A thousand people marched on the secret police headquarters demanding removal of the communist Red Star. When the secret police commander pulled out his pistol and fired in the air as a signal, his men opened fire from the building with machine guns and hand grenades, killing at least 50 people who were blown to pieces. Survivors retrieved weapons from the local army base, besieged the building, and lynched two young secret police officers who remained.
real_qa.requete: Moson Magyarovar secret police massacre October 1956

real_qa.q: Why did Nikita Khrushchev reverse his decision to withdraw Soviet troops from Hungary on October 31, 1956?
real_qa.r: Khrushchev reversed the withdrawal decision because reports showed the Communist Party had collapsed, factories shut down, and newspapers were taken over by rebels. He feared this would encourage American, British, and French imperialists to interpret it as Soviet weakness and attack elsewhere. He also received pressure from other Warsaw Pact countries worried that multi-party elections in Hungary would spread to Poland and Czechoslovakia.
real_qa.requete: Khrushchev Hungary October 31 1956 Soviet intervention decision

real_qa.q: What massacre occurred at Budapest Communist Party headquarters on October 30, 1956?
real_qa.r: Revolutionaries laid siege to the Budapest municipal Communist Party headquarters occupied by secret police and party officials. After secret police fired on the crowd hitting bystanders, a massive gun battle ensued. While the Budapest party boss tried to broker a ceasefire, insurgents broke in and shot him and his bodyguards. Young army officers and secret police were then led outside and shot at point-blank range in full view of photographers, with 23 killed, their bodies beaten and strung up from trees and lampposts.
real_qa.requete: Budapest Communist Party headquarters massacre October 30 1956

real_qa.q: What did the New York Times report about Hungarian victory on October 30, 1956?
real_qa.r: The New York Times correspondent began his report home with the words: 'the Hungarian people seem to have won their revolution,' reflecting the sense of national euphoria as Hungarians achieved new political parties, independent newspapers, and freedom from Communist one-party rule.
real_qa.requete: New York Times Hungarian revolution October 30 1956

October 24, 1956: Red Army ordered to move into Budapest, losing 5 tanks and 120 men on first day
October 26, 1956: At least 50 people killed at Moson Magyarovar secret police headquarters massacre
October 30, 1956: 23 young officers and secret police shot and lynched at Budapest Communist Party headquarters
October 31, 1956: Imre Nagy announced 'the revolution of which you were the heroes has been won'
November 1, 1956: US Secretary of State John Foster Dulles briefed President Eisenhower that Soviet troops had definitively left Budapest
